summary: Introduces a set of specifications for email addresses and headers that use people's own names and scripts, not just plain ASCII. The changes include an SMTP extension and header syntax that allows UTF-8 text, plus a discussion of deployment issues. It is an overview and framework for the series. It was replaced by RFC 6530.

plainLanguage.summary: Email used to only handle English-style letters. This explains how to let people write their names in their own alphabet.

questions: how to support non-english email addresses
can email addresses contain non-ascii characters
subtitle: The roadmap for letting email addresses and headers use people's own names and scripts, in UTF-8.

tldr.problem: The domain part of an email address can already be internationalized, but the local part is limited to a subset of 7-bit ASCII, so people cannot use their own names in their own scripts.
tldr.mechanism: A set of experimental specifications adds an SMTP extension (UTF8SMTP) that allows UTF-8 in addresses and selected headers, requires 8BITMIME, and optionally supports downgrading to ASCII.
tldr.outcome: This overview and framework was replaced by RFC 6530. Related work in the series is updated by RFC 5336.

today: RFC 4952 is obsoleted by RFC 6530 and is also updated by RFC 5336. It was an Informational overview published in July 2007.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
To use internationalized email addresses, both the domain part and the local part must be internationalized. The domain part already is, through IDNA (RFC 3490), but the mailbox name is restricted to a subset of 7-bit ASCII. MIME can carry non-ASCII data and RFC 2047 encoding can put it into a display name, but display-name data is invisible in the message envelope and is not part of the address.

The RFC argues that internationalizing only the domain name has little value on its own. Users prefer addresses that look like names or initials, and the addresses must be handled consistently everywhere they occur. Patches and workarounds are not adequate; the goal is a fully internationalized email environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your name could only be spelled with letters from another country's alphabet. This plan fixes that for email addresses, so people can use their own letters.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
The umbrella name for the work is UTF8SMTP. An address is all-ASCII if every character is ASCII, and non-ASCII (an i18n-address) if any character is not. These two sets are mutually exclusive, and together they make up the set of all UTF8SMTP addresses.

An ASCII user only uses and can only generate all-ASCII addresses. An i18mail user has one or more non-ASCII addresses. The RFC stresses there is no such thing as an "i18mail message"; the term applies only to users, their agents and their capabilities. The final delivery MTA is the SMTP server that controls the format of local parts and may interpret them.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives names to the kinds of addresses and people involved, such as ASCII-only and non-ASCII, so everyone talks about the same thing.

sections.title: The SMTP Extension and UTF-8 Headers
sections.content:
The framework covers several companion documents: an SMTP extension for internationalized addresses, email headers in UTF-8, in-transit downgrading, IMAP and POP extensions, delivery notifications, and usage scenarios.

The UTF8SMTP SMTP extension permits UTF-8 strings in both local parts and domain names, permits selective use of UTF-8 in headers, requires the server to advertise 8BITMIME and the client to support 8-bit transmission, and provides information to support downgrading. Header field names themselves stay in ASCII.

The guiding principles are:

  • When the left side of an address has non-ASCII characters, using punycode on the right side is discouraged, to keep processing consistent.
  • A relay must either recognize the format through an ESMTP option, pick an ASCII-only address and downgrade, or reject the message or return a non-delivery notification.
  • Charsets other than UTF-8 are prohibited in addresses and headers.

Conformance requires implementing the SMTP extension and the UTF-8 header specification. Downgrading support is not required, but if implemented it MUST be implemented as specified.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail systems that understand the new letters tell each other so. They all use one standard way of writing letters, called UTF-8, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: Downgrading for Older Systems
sections.content:
When a client that needs UTF8SMTP meets a server that lacks it, there are two choices. The message can be rejected or bounced back so the sender resubmits with traditional addresses and headers, and this option MAY always be chosen. Or the message can be downgraded in transit, which requires an all-ASCII address from some source. An optional extension parameter can carry an alternate address.

If a UTF8SMTP-capable client is sending a message that is entirely ASCII, it SHOULD send it whether or not the server announces the extension.

Downgrading can also happen before or during submission, where the user has the most options, or after final delivery. A final delivery server MAY downgrade stored messages or mark messages that use the extensions, and if so SHOULD provide a way to recover the original form without information loss.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiving mail system is too old to read the new letters, the sender can either give up and try with a plain address, or swap in a simpler address along the way.

sections.title: Open Issues and Experiments
sections.content:
The RFC lists issues the series does not settle: the mailto: URI scheme may need changes, delivery notifications need updates, email addresses are used as identifiers on many sites that may not cope, and signed or encrypted messages cannot be upgraded from RFC 2047 form without breaking signatures or needing keys. Other uses of local parts, such as building vanity host names, and non-standard storage formats that assume US-ASCII headers, may also break.

It also names two experimental questions: what restrictions such as character lists or normalization should apply to local parts, and how useful downgrading will turn out to be in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors admit there are loose ends, like signed letters and old tools, and say they will learn more by trying the plan out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Allowing more characters raises risks such as IDN homograph spoofing, which can also happen in local parts. The fix of forcing displayed names into normalized lower case works for domain names but not for local parts, which are case sensitive. Confusable characters are a particular problem for addresses copied from business cards.

Downgrading is another risk: anything that transforms one address into another is a point where spoofing can occur, and code must not assume an authenticated binding between an internationalized address and its ASCII form. New forms of malformed messages could be read differently by filters and mail clients. The work also affects header-signing systems such as DKIM, and PKI certificates that contain email addresses. The RFC concludes that the mechanisms do not in general raise new security issues, but they require review of confusable characters.
sections.plainLanguage: Letters from different alphabets can look the same, so a trickster could fake an address. Mail systems must stay careful when they swap addresses around.
